title: The ladder (Genesis 28:10–22)
hook: a runaway sleeps on a stone and wakes saying the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stolen blessing, berakhah: goatskins, a blind father, and Esau's bitter cry. Your line was the bible doesn't hide it. Did you take your honest step? Today, the liar is on the run. Day three hundred fifty-six.

Jacob has the blessing. He also has a brother who wants him dead. So he leaves home with almost nothing, walking toward Haran, his uncle's country, alone. By sunset he's somewhere in the hills, nowhere in particular, no inn, no friend, no tent. He picks up a stone, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground. A night far from home, in a bus station or a hospital chair or a strange city, after something you did went badly wrong: that's this night. It's the last place anyone expects to meet God.
screen: `THE BLESSING, AND A BROTHER'S RAGE.` → `ALONE IN THE HILLS AT SUNSET.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: First, the dream. A ladder, or a stairway, stands on the earth, its top reaching heaven, and the angels of God are going up and down on it. Going up first, then down, as if they were already here. And the Lord stands above it. Second, the promise. God doesn't scold Jacob for the lie. God repeats the promise to Abraham: the land, descendants like the dust of the earth, and in you all the families of the earth will be blessed. And then something new, just for him: I will keep you wherever you go, and I will not leave you. Third, the waking. In the Douay-Rheims: "And when Jacob awaked out of sleep, he said: Indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not." And then, trembling: "this is no other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven." He sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel, which in Hebrew means house of God. A nowhere place in the hills, renamed. Fourth, where the Church hears it. In the Gospel of John, Jesus tells Nathanael he'll see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Christian tradition reads Christ as the ladder itself, the meeting of heaven and earth. And in the Church's traditional chant for the dedication of a church, the Mass opens with Jacob's words in Latin: Terribilis est locus iste, how awesome is this place. A building, consecrated with the words of a runaway who slept on a rock.
screen: `ANGELS GOING UP, THEN DOWN.` · `I WILL NOT LEAVE YOU.` · `BETHEL: HOUSE OF GOD.` · `CHRIST AS THE LADDER.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where God was unnoticed. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the past week. Look for a place or a moment you passed through without a thought: a bus ride, a hard conversation, a waiting room, a sink full of dishes, a sleepless hour. Pick one. Now replay it slowly, as if it were Bethel. What was there that you missed? A kindness, a quiet, a person, a gift. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words about it: the Lord was in this place. If not, simply notice what was there. The bell holds the time.
The ladder. Jacob's dream at Bethel: a stairway between earth and heaven, angels on it, God above, and a promise: I will not leave you.
Your line: and I knew it not. Today, in one ordinary place, a kitchen, a car, a hallway, stop for three breaths and look again. Day three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: The traditional entrance chant for the dedication of a church, Terribilis est locus iste, takes Jacob's words at Bethel, and Genesis 28:11–18 is among the readings the Church offers for that rite.

original.note: Hebrew: Bethel, house of God. Jacob's name for the place he slept on a stone.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ladder to climb up to heaven.
what it means: in the worst night of a liar's life, God comes down and promises to stay, and an ordinary place becomes the house of God.
what a scholar hears: the angels ascend first, then descend; Bethel, house of God; Christ in John 1:51 as the ladder.

28:15 paraphrased ('I will be thy keeper wherever thou goest, and I will not leave thee'); confirm against the Douay-Rheims before any quotation marks are added.
Terribilis est locus iste: the traditional introit for the dedication of a church (and its anniversary). 'For centuries' — confirm; the current Missal's entrance antiphons may differ.
Genesis 28:11–18 as an option in the lectionary for the dedication of a church; confirm.
'Ladder, or stairway': Hebrew sullam; confirm. Practice keeps 'if you pray' invitation.
